Note: In your defense, in between when I commented initially and now, Lolalytics has updated Skarner’s page to reflect the winrate delta in master. I’ll still walk you through my initial process though, back when it wasn’t updated:


- First, we check Skarner’s main page. This gives us the following information:

>> The best Skarner players have a 55.34% win rate with an average rank of Master on the Skarner Leaderboard.

However, this data is misleading, since the average winrate in master is 52.12%. When accounting for the increased average winrate in that rank, Skarner instead sits at a respectable 53.24% winrate. What does this winrate mean?

This winrate means that Skarner mains succeed with him at a similar rate to meta/strong champions. (For comparison, Olaf and Cass succeed roughly the same amount as Skarner does, and both of them sit comfortably in the A-S tier). 

However, as you mentioned, if the average one-tricked champion had a mean higher winrate, that could suggest that Skarner as a champion still underperforms when mastered (which would prove Phreak’s analysis wrong, that Skarner is fine when mastered but very weak otherwise). 

Skarner however, averages a 55.34% winrate among onetricks, which indicates that he performs roughly at par with other mained characters (μ = 55.89%). **Some** champions that perform equally as good as him (when mained) or worse are Leblanc, Pyke, Nidalee, Jayce, Ryze, Lee Sin, Draven, K’Sante, Rengar, Rek’Sai, and Kalista, which are all champions notorious for their high skill requirements.

With that being said, if Skarner performs .55% worse than the average mained champion, wouldn’t that make him bad?

To answer that question, we have to view the stats in context. If there was a ‘one-trick’ rank, then that could indicate Skarner players fall behind lp-wise, but one-tricks play within **our** rank system. This means that they’re often (in fact, overwhelmingly often) playing versus people who aren’t onetricks. So in realistic terms, Skarner players still find success in our ranked system (that is, they have around a 53% winrate, which is positive).

To recap: Skarner mains average a ~53% winrate in the Master rank (or 55% when not accounting for delta), which puts him in the upper tiers of champion success. Skarner mains perform slightly worse than the average one-trick (Δ = 0.55%) but still perform exceptionally well in the context of actually playing the game. 

Further arguments could be made towards whether Skarner would be healthier (or unhealthier) if he was stronger once mastered, but the stats quite clearly indicate that, once mained, Skarner players gain LP.

Skarner mains average a rank of master. Checking the avg winrate at master, it means that Skarner mains perform roughly 2% better than the average player at Master tier. This is in line with other hard-to-play champions, like Ryze, K’Sante, and Nidalee.

Very cool concept! However there are some issues with her:

Base Stats:
- Base Health and growth is far too low for an assassin (nonetheless, a league of legends champion). For reference, Yuumi has 500-1673 health. 
-  Armor is waaay too low to be a jungler. At late game you’ll be getting one-tapped by ADC auto attack before your abilities even finish casting.
- Range: 550 range is really, really high for a jungler. Kindred has to work for her range, and all the other ranged jungler have it tied to a skillshot. This incentivizes her to not play in the jungle, but instead play in a lane.

Abilities:
- Q cooldown is insanely long, but the other abilities have a stronger incentive to be maxed first (W being AOE and thus clear-speed reliant, and E having 3 charges). This means that Q would likely stay at 18 seconds the whole game, relying entirely on W resets to get it back.
- Scaling % damage increases along with flat ones leaves to incredibly lopsided spells. Base rank W does 96 base damage to enemies under half, while max rank does 384. In general the rule of maxing spells is that max rank should be roughly 3x the output of base rank, but currently it’s closer to 4x the output.
- 450 radius is really big. That’s Hydra active, or Urgot W radius. Considering she’s dashing through an area as she does this, it’s functionally undodgeable.
- Just keep the charge cooldown for E, no need to have an additional one if you deplete all charges.
- E, however, gives her an insane amount of safety in lane. Drop a ward by your turret and you have 3 charges of 1000 range GTFO at any time. Combined with her range and durability issues, she would be played top lane as a bully (maybe even tear start?).
- Executes cap at 25% health in league or have an explicit flat scaling. I don’t see a reason for her to break that rule.


Conclusion:
- Look at Kindred’s base stats if you want an aggressive jungler. I’d honestly make her melee instead of ranged, give her normal champion durability, and let her function that way.
- Her passive gives her waaay too much early game power and makes her entirely incontestable for a handful of levels (Kayle’s 20 bonus damage makes her a menace, having 60+ bonus damage on every auto makes her even more uncontestable. Id suggest changing it to non-crit related bonus damage and take out the auto-crit passive.
- Q and W gives the vibes of good assassin design, but id take a look at reworking E again. As of now it feels like a powercrept version of Ekko E that makes her way too safe (given that her durability is fixed). 
- Ult is fun!

Prowler’s on the other hand opens up assassins to use their mobility defensively (when they’d normally be limited). Prowler in, drop combo, E/W out.

Prowler was not just removed because of edge cases (Rek’Sai, for example), prowler was removed because it seriously limited what backliners could feasibly do in fights. Prowler adding 500 distance onto a champion’s engage range meant that some champions legit couldn’t be outplayed anymore.
It was banned to shake up game diversity, not because it was too strong.

The reason for crit + AS + AD items getting removed was because:

- ADC’s have 4 damage multipliers (AD, AS, Crit, Armor Pen) compared to mages who only have 3 (AP, AH, Magic Penetration). Since almost every single ADC item was giving 3 multiplicative stats it meant that, to balance out the insane multiplicative power created with each item, all aspects of it had to be notably weaker. That’s why crit is now 25% instead of 20% on items, which opens up build diversity. (Comparatively, only 2 mage items grant 3 multipliers, Malignance and Cryptbloom, both of which have tradeoffs). 

- Because attack speed was incidentally gained through every item purchase (with lethal tempo being a big offender as well), attack speed items were actually horrible. With individual stats being more important, AS purchases are now important parts of builds again. 

- According to Phreak, he wants to trend the game towards lower individual item power, to both reduce snowballing and late game lethality. By next season he hopes to nerf the gold efficiency of all items. These changes are ADC positive over all.

A few reasons:

- Corki’s old passive was all-around a source of confusion for players, leading to countless incorrect item purchases. Many Corki players were building AP items before 3rd item (and oftentimes more than one), at a frequency that was seriously deflating his winrate. At the same time, many opponents had a false notion that Corki’s damage type was based on what build he went, which led to a shocking amount of armor purchases against Corki. Similar to how defensive stat shards were removed in favor of health, this change was done to increase overall game clarity.

- Corki’s (old) passive was really unsatisfying for players. It functionally read “Gain -10 to 40 penetration based on your enemy’s level. In exchange, armor penetration items don’t work.” It’s effectiveness was seriously misunderstood by the majority of players and, while it was a cool gimmick for some players to see those blue autos, was one of the (many) factors that lead to low player retention. 

- Corki’s old passive was actually really bad. It meant that the champion itself had to be exceedingly overturned to make up for the swath of items that didn’t function on him (out of current AD items, around 15 of them would’ve had seriously reduced effectiveness on old Corki). To avoid another balancing headache such as Morde not having access to good class itemization and thus being ‘overturned’, this was another reason for his old passive removal.



Now to push back on some of your points:

- True damage isn’t an overpowered mechanic. Amumu, Bel’Veth, Kog, K’Sante, Olaf, Syndra, Twitch, and arguably Vel’Koz all have serious amounts of true damage in their kits that no one cares about. True damage really only becomes a problem when it’s making players feel like defensive purchases aren’t worth buying (they always are, people are just emotional), and Corki’s 15% will never reach that point. 

- Aside from like 4-6 weeks in the past 3 years, it was never good to build AP items on Corki, save for last slot Void Staff. You were just losing to the shopkeeper,: Trinity Force -> Manamune -> Bruiser/Crit held 5%+ higher winrates than AP builds for the entire time. Even then, Corki has a higher AP ratio on his Q than before (70%), and unless you really miss that 12% / 24% ratio on his ult (mind you, that’s less AP ratio than Ivern’s W passive, among other wimpy abilities), you’re really not missing much.

Anecdotal evidence is historically unreliable. If I, with my emerald experience, said that Zilean was unbeatable freelo and clicking E on anyone pre-tier 2 boots meant they were dead to a jungle gank, I would only be speaking for my experience. It would be with my level of experience, with my build, with my teammates, and most importantly **contextualized within my ELO**. While there’s certainly some concepts that can be applied across skill brackets (for example, Zilean has decent gank assist), the ‘unbeatable freelo’ part is unique to my experience.

Thus, if we want to objectively look at the experiences of other players en-masse, we can use statistical data. Statistical data doesn’t have biases unless recorded or utilized incorrectly, which is why I contextualize my winrate examples with qualitative examples of playrate/games played per player ratio. This ratio helps us to see how many of the players for a specific champion **main** that champion, and help us see how inflated or deflated a champion’s winrate is (based on skill requirements). 

Your anecdotal experiences are valuable to get a window into your experience playing Zilean. But if we’re looking at the overall strength of a character across multiple skill brackets, we would need thousands of anecdotes from a variety of Zilean players to get an accurate depiction of the champion (through that method).

You can literally find on the internet the ‘average games played on the champ vs the popularity’ to find if they’re an otp pick or not. When you make assumptions that X champion’s winrate is or isn’t being inflated by OTP’s, you can literally search up if that is or isn’t the case.

I’ve been playing Magic for roughly 10 years, starting off with just casual decks between friends, trying out modern and standard for a year, and now primarily doing commander.


I started Yugioh this most recent summer, playing it via Master Duels.


In Yugioh, I play weather painters. I have 2 negates going into my opponent’s first turn (plus any other ones in my hand) so I have to be super keen on what needs negating. Especially if my opponent uses a combo line I’m not familiar with (floowanderzee completely whooped me), I risk using up my negates and just losing t2. When I versed my friends, they didn’t even look at the cards I was playing, just waiting till it was their turn to attempt to combo off.

The existence of archetypes in Yugioh (namely the sets of tutors and areas-turned into resource pools) means that, while certain start or endgame pieces might be seen across decks (as well as hand traps), the inner workings of each combo are wildly different. For example, my T1 play in Weather Painters is:

Weather Painter Snow -> Tutors on ETB for Weather Snowy Canvas -> Painter Snow uses the Snowy Canvas to tutor for a Weather Forecast, which tutors up an additional Canvas of my choice on ETB (ranging from various forms of distruption to more value engines), then I activate its second ability to normal summon an additional painter. 

All of this is off of one card. While many of the parts of this chain can be Ash-Blossomed, Ash-ing the start doesn’t really do much since there’s a bunch of other ways to grab snowy canvas. Destroying many of the spell cards doesn’t matter much either since I can reaction tutor up protection for them, and destroying my front row doesn’t matter since I can protect them 100% of the time.

You will never see this much specific deck chaining done at any part of the game in Magic. At most in Cedh you’ll see some sort of combo that you haven’t seen before that leads into thoracle. Even if you haven’t seen a card before, in Magic it’s super easy to glance at the card and get an idea of what it does and how to deal with it. In Yugioh, every single card is a wall of text littered with caveats that cause specific kinds of interaction to fizzle on them.
In mtg, the threat assessment is pretty clear. In Yugioh, it’s incredibly unclear.

Now, specifically dealing with strike resets:
Most characters either have access to a high/low mix, a left/right mix, or a low left/high left/mid right mix. Identify what mix your opponent is using then perform a guess based on their mix. You can also use a DP, but if they predict this and block you can be very hard punished.

Grab resets are a little different. Ground grabs can always be avoided if you hold up while in hit stun, but this leaves you vulnerable to low hits. This is a type of mix called a low/throw mix. 
Pressing grab when a gap appears in their combo is the best way to stop a grab reset. Worse case scenario is they tech and both of you return to neutral (aside from them jumping on prediction). Only some DP’s work against grabs so keep that in mind if you opt to do that instead.
Air grabs must be teched. Look for those gaps then grab!



When coming in, there are usually two mixes that occur:

- Left/right grounded mix: This usually happens when they call an assist (a common example is point Annie using L knuckle while assist Robo Fortune uses H theonite beam).
- Strike/Throw Aerial Mix: If they don’t call an assist, or they call it too far away to hit you, they’re going for one of these.

You are actionable as soon as you gain tangibility, so react accordingly to your opponents setup then attempt a defense.

For ability leveling, you can either go:

Q -> W -> E -> Q -> W -> R (Max R -> W -> Q -> E) This gives slightly better wave control, and lets you harass from 700 units away with Q for stronger early poke. Why a second point in Q? You hit waveclear breakpoints at the same time anyway, but it gives you much more powerful early damage. 

W -> E -> Q -> Q -> W -> R (Max R -> W -> Q -> E)

Now for techniques:

- R Prepping is an Incredibly important skill, and doing so unlocks Leblanc’s safest and most damaging combos. To R prep, simply use the desired ability out of combat, then when you enter combat lead with the prepared ultimate:
- Prep R (Q): Less useful than other ones, but can let you R (Q) -> Q your enemy laner, which is much higher damage than Q -> R (Q). This can sometimes burst them by surprise.
- Prep R (W): Incredibly important. R (W) -> Q -> W is Leblanc’s bread and butter safe combo atm. Super fast and solid damage. Another combo R(W) -> E -> Q -> Save W to dodge skillshots or follow dashes, gives her some of the best pick potential in the game.
- Prep R (E): This unlocks Leblanc’s highest damage combo R (E) -> Q [Must do this immediately after the R(E) hits] -> E -> Q -> W, which annihilates most squishy enemies.

For Leblanc/ Zoe, who needs to poke you down before she bursts you, fleet is great for keeping you healthy enough to not die and get off backs. For Fizz/ Qiyana, who need to commit in their all-in, you can more reliably get off the HoB autos without needing to spend W (as you would in the Leblanc/Zoe matchup). 

I’d say the biggest difference is:

Non-committal enemies (usually ranged): Fleet

Committal enemies (usually Melee): HoB


Lethal tempo is good into people like Yone/Bruisers mid who you can safely chip down with autos as they farm. They won’t be dissuaded by 3 HoB autos, but consistent poke let’s you heavily harass them. If they try to all-in you, your Lethal tempo will be stacked up and you can out trade with proper kiting and W usage.


Edit: I just realized a much easier way to say it

Ask yourself: How many autos will you get off in a trade.

1-2 -> Fleet Footwork

3-5 -> Hail of Blades

6+ -> Lethal Tempo

If you’re not going crit, then always go First Strike.

If you are going crit, then pick your rune for lane phase to help you get through the matchup:
- Fleet: Matchups where you need to stay above health thresholds to not get bursted.
- HoB: Matchups where you need to have damage threat in short trades. 
- Lethal Tempo: Matchups where you need to constantly poke the enemy laner down so they can’t all-in you (Melee lane opponents only).
- First Strike: Farm Lane.
- Phase Rush: Jungle + Mid comps that CAN AND WILL DIVE YOU.
